title: Calling Out
paragraphs: Every Saturday, long before the rest of the city was awake, the market under the railway arches burst into life. Traders heaved crates from their vans, striped awnings flapped in the breeze, and the air filled with the smells of fresh bread, roasting coffee and ripe fruit. In the middle of it all stood Grandad's fruit and vegetable stall, and behind it stood Grandad, whose booming voice could be heard from one end of the market to the other.

'Sweet, juicy pears!' he would bellow. 'Strawberries as red as rubies!' But this Saturday, when Grandad opened his mouth, only a croak came out, like the creak of a rusty gate. He had caught a terrible cold. 'You'll have to do the calling today,' he whispered to Amir, pressing a hand to his throat.

Amir's heart sank. He loved helping at the stall: he could stack oranges into perfect pyramids and count out change faster than anyone. Shouting in front of strangers, however, was a different matter altogether. He took a deep breath and opened his mouth. 'Apples,' he said. It came out as barely more than a whisper. A woman with a pushchair walked straight past without even glancing at the stall.

Opposite them, Aisha was bellowing about her fresh mackerel, and a crowd had gathered around the fish stall. By eleven o'clock, Grandad had sold only three bags of potatoes, and in the warm sunshine the strawberries were beginning to soften. Grandad said nothing, but Amir noticed him glancing anxiously at the strawberries and then at the cash box, which was almost empty.

Amir stared at the strawberries. Then he remembered the silly rhymes he made up at bedtime to make his little sister giggle. Before he could change his mind, he dragged an empty crate to the front of the stall and climbed on to it. His knees were wobbling, but he cupped his hands around his mouth. 'Strawberries, strawberries, juicy and sweet! The tastiest treat that you ever could eat!'

His voice squeaked on the last word, and his cheeks burned. But a man with a newspaper stopped and chuckled, and a girl tugged at her mother's sleeve and pointed. Amir tried another. 'Potatoes for chips and onions for stew, and a big shiny apple for someone like you!' This time, his voice did not squeak at all.

Soon a small crowd had gathered in front of the stall. People laughed and clapped, and children shouted out fruit and vegetables for Amir to rhyme, from bananas to cabbages. Amir made up a rhyme for every one, while Grandad filled paper bags as fast as his hands could move. Even Aisha wandered over from the fish stall to listen, wiping her hands on her apron.

By two o'clock, the stall was almost bare. Every strawberry had gone, and the only thing left was one knobbly potato that nobody seemed to want. Grandad squeezed Amir's shoulder. 'You've found your voice,' he croaked, and his eyes were shining.

The next Saturday, Grandad's cold had gone, and his booming voice was back. As the first shoppers drifted through the arches, he filled his lungs to shout. Then he stopped, winked at Amir and pushed the empty crate towards him with his foot.

questions.prompt:
At the start of the story, Amir is too shy to call out, but by the end he is confident.
Explain how the writer shows this change, using evidence from the text.
questions.model: At first, Amir is nervous. When he tries to call out, 'It came out as barely more than a whisper', and when he climbs on to the crate, 'His knees were wobbling'. When a man chuckles and a girl points at his first rhyme, he feels encouraged and tries another. By the end he is confident: 'This time, his voice did not squeak at all', and he 'made up a rhyme for every one' while a crowd gathered.
points: Shows that Amir is shy or nervous at first, with evidence, e.g. 'It came out as barely more than a whisper' or 'His knees were wobbling'.
Shows that he becomes confident, with evidence, e.g. 'This time, his voice did not squeak at all' or he 'made up a rhyme for every one'.
Explains what helped him to change, e.g. people stopped, laughed and clapped at his rhymes, so he felt encouraged.

A shy boy finds his voice by making up rhymes and helps Grandad to sell almost everything on the stall.
